title: Aquinas, again
tomorrow: what's the very first word of Benedict's Rule?

cards: A pickup game after school. A freshman misses an easy pass, and the yelling is out before you can stop it. Afterward, the quiet thought: maybe holy people just aren't built like me.

Maybe being good means turning the competitive part off. Thomas Aquinas, the Dominican friar who wrote the Summa, gives a different answer, and it's one line long: grace does not destroy nature, it perfects it.

teach.b: Start where Aquinas starts: what you are is good. Genesis says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, "God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good."
Sin wounds that goodness, but it doesn't turn it into something else. So when grace comes, God's own life given freely, it doesn't swap you out for a calmer person.
It heals what's wounded and finishes what's there, the way a coach doesn't hand you someone else's legs but trains the ones you have. A sharp mind becomes a mind that seeks truth.
A big heart becomes a heart that loves well. And a competitive streak? Paul didn't ask athletes to stop.

teach.h: SO RUN THAT YOU MAY OBTAIN.
teach.b: He wrote to the Corinthians: "So run that you may obtain." Here's the one to tell a friend: Aquinas says not all anger is sin.
In the Summa he argues that anger ruled by reason, aimed at what's truly wrong, can even be good; anger that runs ahead of reason is the problem.
So grace doesn't delete the fire. It teaches the fire where to burn. That doesn't excuse the yelling.
The pass was missed, not a wrong done, and the anger ran ahead of reason. Grace works there too: an apology, a cooler head next time, a drive that lifts the freshman instead of flattening her.
The same nature, perfected, not erased.

how: Catholics honor Thomas Aquinas as a Doctor of the Church and patron of students; his teaching that grace builds on nature shapes how the Church speaks of virtue, sports, work and every human gift.

games.q: your teammate is fiercely competitive and wonders if she should quit sports to be a better Christian. what does Aquinas's line suggest?
o: keep the drive, and let grace aim it at the good.
quit: holiness means switching the drive off.
nothing changes: her nature is fine just as it is.
games.why: grace does not destroy nature but perfects it. the drive stays; grace heals what's wounded in it and points it somewhere good.

practice: Count three things about how you're made: a strength, a quirk, and something people have called too much.
For each one, if you pray, you can say a quiet thank you to God for it; if not, name each one as good, the way Genesis does, and let it stay.

wordCard.voice: Aquinas. Thomas Aquinas, friar and teacher, who saw grace finishing nature instead of fighting it.

carryVoice: Your line: grace perfects, finishing what God already called very good, competitive streak included. See you tomorrow.
